spec.title: Accepted vs sent rate (req/s)
spec.description: Accepted = answers 202 (k6 counter b11_resp_202, added by this experiment's script, so it exists only after a k6 run). Sent = every answer plus dropped iterations. In the soak both should sit on the offered 3000. A slow slide of the accepted line is the throughput decay of the hypothesis; at 70% of the knee I do not expect it. In the 6000 probes the accepted line IS the capacity: compare the plateau of cap_start with cap_end. Surprising: accepted below sent in the soak (503s or dropped iterations).

spec.title: Latency seen by k6: p50 / p99
spec.description: Time from k6 sending a request to the answer. The main panel: the hypothesis says p99 grows with the table and gets spikes at checkpoints. Look for a slow upward trend in p99 over the 60 minutes and for regular peaks (a checkpoint every few minutes). Native histogram from k6 remote write. k6 series are not marked stale after a run, the last value can linger for minutes.

spec.title: Events inserted by the server (req/s) and errors
spec.description: Server-side count of rows it inserted (ep_events_inserted_total) next to the 503 and 'other' answers k6 saw (counters added by this experiment's script). Inserted should equal accepted. Surprising: any 503 or 'other' in the soak; the pool timeout (2 s) turns into 503.

spec.title: Size of table events and its indexes
spec.description: Heap (table) and all indexes of events, from the postgres exporter, plus shared_buffers (Postgres' own cache) and the container memory limit is 2 GB (see env.txt). Growth should be a straight line while the rate is fixed. The moment the index line passes shared_buffers is where I expect the cache hit ratio to start falling. Surprising: a bend in the growth line (the rate changed, or autovacuum).

spec.title: Checkpoints per minute
spec.description: timed = the 5 minute timer fired, requested = WAL grew close to max_wal_size (1 GB) first. At about 2 MB/s of WAL I expect requested checkpoints to dominate. Surprising: more requested checkpoints later in the run than at the start (WAL per row grew, see the WAL panel). The scrape interval limits how small the window can be.

spec.title: Who writes the dirty buffers (buffers/s)
spec.description: Buffers (8 KB pages) written by the checkpointer, by the background writer (clean) and by the backends themselves (backend). Backend writes mean the insert had to write a page itself because it needed a free buffer: it adds to the request time. I expect checkpoint writes to rise with the index size; surprising: a backend line that grows with time.

spec.title: Buffer cache hit ratio
spec.description: hit / (hit + read) per second. 'database' is the whole eventpulse database, 'events indexes' only the indexes of events. A read here is a page not found in shared_buffers; it may still come from the OS page cache, so this is not a disk read yet (the disk panel shows real reads). I expect a fall as the random uuid primary key outgrows the 128 MB; surprising: no fall at all.

spec.title: WAL bytes per event and full-page images per event
spec.description: WAL per inserted row (about 730 B in B6) and full-page images per row. A full-page image is a whole 8 KB page written to WAL the first time it is changed after a checkpoint. A random index touches a different page every insert, so once the index has more pages than inserts per checkpoint, FPI per row rises and so does WAL per row. WAL and FPI come from the textfile exporter started by run.sh (ep_pg_wal_*). Surprising: a flat line.

spec.title: Time inside the pool connection: INSERT p50 / p99
spec.description: Server-side time of the INSERT on an acquired connection (includes the COMMIT wait for the WAL flush). It is the part of the request that Postgres owns. With the pool of 25 it also sets the capacity: 25 / hold time. Surprising: p99 far above p50 with regular peaks (checkpoint), or p50 itself rising.

spec.title: Pool wait p99 and requests waiting for a connection
spec.description: How long a request waits for a free pool connection (p99), and how many are waiting right now. At 70% of capacity the queue should be short; it grows fast when the hold time rises, because the pool is the limit (B1 to B3). Surprising: waiting above a few for long stretches.

spec.title: Autovacuum runs on events (cumulative) and live rows
spec.description: events never gets updates or deletes, but since Postgres 13 inserts alone also start autovacuum (to set visibility bits). Each run reads the table and writes WAL. Steps in the first line are autovacuum runs; look for a latency bump next to a step. Rows: the statistics collector's estimate of live rows.

spec.title: Disk busy and throughput (host disk)
spec.description: Busy = fraction of time the disk had a request in flight (1 = 100%). Read and written bytes/s on the nvme device (the disk of the Postgres volume, see env.txt). Reads that appear here are the cache misses that went all the way to the disk. B1 saw this disk near 97% busy with commit flushes, so a rising busy line means the checkpoint writes and index reads compete with the WAL flush. The device regex is for this machine.

spec.title: Postgres container: CPU and disk bytes
spec.description: CPU cores used by the Postgres container (the container is limited to 2) and its disk read/write MB/s from its cgroup (textfile exporter started by run.sh). Surprising: CPU near 2 cores means Postgres is the limit, not the pool.

spec.title: Postgres memory and OS page cache
spec.description: Memory charged to the Postgres container (it includes page cache, limit 2 GB) and the host page cache. The container memory rises to its limit as files are written and read, then the kernel reclaims; the point where table plus index no longer fit in it is where cache misses become disk reads.

spec.title: CPU of the pinned groups (busy fraction)
spec.description: 1 minus idle for each pinned core group (server, Postgres, k6). Postgres has 4 cores in the cpuset but the container is limited to 2 CPUs, so its busy fraction stays at about half. Surprising: a line that climbs steadily over the hour.

spec.title: Node process CPU (cores)
spec.description: CPU of the ingest-api process, user and system. About 0.17 ms per request (B1) gives about 0.5 core at 3000 req/s. Surprising: growth over time (the server should not care about the table size).

spec.title: k6 dropped iterations (must be 0 in the soak)
spec.description: Requests k6 planned but could not start. In the soak and the fresh control this must stay 0, otherwise the run is discarded. In the two 6000 probes dropped iterations are expected (the offered rate is above the capacity). k6 series are not marked stale after a run. Built-in k6 series have no exp label, so they are matched by testid starting with b11-.

spec.title: k6 VUs vs max
spec.description: Virtual users in use against the maximum. In the soak it should be a few tens. Close to the maximum means the generator is running out (and dropped iterations follow).

spec.title: Free disk space on / (guard: 10 GB)
spec.description: Free space of the filesystem that holds the Postgres volume. run.sh stops the run if it falls below 10 GB (MIN_FREE_GB). The soak writes table plus index at roughly 100 MB/min; WAL is recycled. Surprising: a fall that is much steeper than the growth of the table.

spec.title: Event loop lag p99 (server)
spec.description: How late the Node timer fires. Above about 50 ms the server's own thread is busy and latency is not coming from Postgres. Surprising: any rise over time.

spec.title: Requests in flight and open connections (server)
spec.description: http_requests_in_flight is Little's law made visible: rate x time in the server. At 3000 req/s and 6 ms it is about 18. If it climbs during the soak, the answers got slower.

spec.title: 1. The verdict: does the service get slower while the table grows?
2. The mechanism: table size, checkpoints, cache, WAL
3. Resource view: where the cost lands
4. Validity checks: can I trust this run?
EventPulse B11 - Table growth soak
